primary-productivity-s1.title: Gross productivity and respiration in five ecosystems

table.caption: Gross primary productivity (GPP) and plant respiration (R) in five ecosystems, in kcal per square meter per year (invented, rounded data for practice; real values vary widely)

primary-productivity-s2.title: Light and oxygen bottles in a lake

plot.label: Bar chart of dissolved oxygen at the start and after 24 hours in a clear bottle and a dark bottle of lake water, invented data

options: The total rate producers capture energy
The energy left after producers use some for respiration
The energy that reaches the animals at the top of the chain
The rate at which decomposers release CO2 from dead matter

why.correct: GPP is the total energy (or carbon) producers capture by photosynthesis in an area per unit of time.
options: Right: the total capture by photosynthesis.
That is net primary productivity (NPP).
Animals at the top get a tiny share of the energy, not GPP.
Decomposer respiration is a different flux.

items.q: Why is net primary productivity (NPP) always smaller than GPP?
options: Producers use some of it in respiration.
Plant-eating animals eat part of the GPP before it is measured.
Sunlight is lost before it reaches the leaves of the plants.
Decomposers break down part of the GPP each night.

why.correct: $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - \text{R}$: the plants’ own respiration uses part of what they capture, leaving NPP as new plant matter.
options: Right: plant respiration is subtracted.
Grazing removes NPP later; it is not why NPP is smaller than GPP.
Light that misses leaves is never counted in GPP.
Decomposers act on dead matter, not on GPP itself.

items.q: A salt marsh has a GPP of 9,000 kcal/m²/yr, and its plants use 5,500 kcal/m²/yr in respiration. What is its NPP?

mistakes.why: You added. NPP is what is left after respiration: GPP minus R.
Subtract respiration from GPP, not GPP from respiration: 9,000 - 5,500.

items.q: A forest’s NPP is 2,000 kcal/m²/yr, and its plants use 4,000 kcal/m²/yr in respiration. Write the setup for its GPP, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: GPP is the total: NPP plus what respiration used, so add.
That is 4,000 - 2,000. GPP = NPP + R: add them.

items.q: Which factor most limits primary productivity in a desert?
options: Water, which is scarce
Sunlight, since deserts are cloudy most days
Carbon dioxide, since desert air lacks it
Temperature, since deserts are cold year-round

why.correct: Deserts get plenty of light, but little water. Plants close leaf pores to save water, which also limits the CO2 they take in, so photosynthesis is slow.
options: Right: water shortage limits photosynthesis.
Deserts are among the sunniest places.
Desert air has the same CO2 as anywhere.
Many deserts are hot; temperature is not the main limit.

items.q: Which ecosystem usually has the highest NPP per square meter?
options: Tropical rainforest
Open ocean
Arctic tundra
Hot desert

why.correct: Warmth, abundant water and year-round light give tropical rainforests (along with swamps, marshes and reefs) the highest NPP per square meter.
options: Right: warm, wet and sunny all year.
The open ocean is low per square meter because surface nutrients are scarce.
Cold and a short growing season limit the tundra.
Lack of water limits deserts.

items.q: Why does more sunlight not always increase primary productivity?
options: Another factor may be limiting.
Plants do not use sunlight for photosynthesis.
Sunlight lowers the amount of CO2 in the air.
More light speeds respiration more than photosynthesis.

why.correct: Productivity is limited by whatever is scarcest: light, water, temperature or nutrients. Adding more of something that is not scarce changes little.
options: Right: the scarcest factor sets the limit.
Photosynthesis is powered by light.
Light does not change atmospheric CO2.
That is not a general rule; light mainly drives photosynthesis.

items.q: A student will grow algae in jars under different amounts of nitrate. Build a testable hypothesis.

why.correct: A directional hypothesis names the change in the independent variable, the direction of the dependent variable and a reason.

specific.frame: If more ___ is added, then algae growth will ___, because nitrogen is ___.

iv.label: Independent variable
options: nitrate
light
water

why.1: The student is changing nitrate, not light.
why.2: Every jar has water; nitrate is what changes.

direction.label: Direction
options: increase
be affected
change

why.1: "Be affected" gives no direction. Say increase or decrease.
why.2: "Change" gives no direction. Say increase or decrease.

because.label: Reason
options: often a limiting nutrient
a gas that blocks light
poisonous to algae

why.1: Dissolved nitrate does not block light.
why.2: Nitrate is a nutrient for algae at these levels.

specific.model: If more nitrate is added, then algae growth will increase, because nitrogen is often the limiting nutrient for algae.

items.q: What is the NPP of the temperate grassland?

mistakes.why: You added GPP and R. NPP is GPP minus R.

items.q: Which ecosystem has the highest NPP?
options: Tropical rainforest
Temperate deciduous forest
Temperate grassland
Open ocean

why.correct: NPP: rainforest 3,200; deciduous forest 2,000; grassland 1,200; desert scrub 150; open ocean 400 kcal/m²/yr.

items.q: What percent of its GPP does the tropical rainforest use in respiration?

mistakes.why: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.
That is the share left as NPP. The question asks for the share used in respiration: R / GPP × 100.

items.q: Which ecosystem has the largest share of its GPP left as NPP?
options: Temperate grassland
Tropical rainforest
Desert scrub
Open ocean

why.correct: NPP as a share of GPP: grassland $1{,}200/2{,}400 = 50\%$; rainforest 42%; deciduous forest 40%; desert scrub 37.5%; open ocean 40%.
options: Right: half of its GPP is left.
Highest NPP, but only about 42% of its GPP is left.
About 37.5% of its GPP is left.
40% of its GPP is left.

items.q: Oxygen fell from 8.0 to 7.4 mg/L in the dark bottle in 24 hours. What was the rate of respiration, in mg/L of oxygen per day?

why.correct: In the dark there is no photosynthesis, so the drop is respiration alone: $8.0 - 7.4 = 0.6$ mg/L per day.

mistakes.why: 1.5 is the change in the clear bottle (net productivity). Respiration is the drop in the dark bottle.

items.q: The rise in the clear bottle (8.0 to 9.5 mg/L) measures which quantity?
options: Net productivity
Gross productivity by itself
Respiration by itself
Decomposition of dead algae

why.correct: In light, algae photosynthesize and respire at once, so the oxygen change is the net: 1.5 mg/L per day.
options: Right: the clear bottle shows the net change.
Gross productivity adds back the respiration measured in the dark bottle.
Respiration alone is the dark bottle.
Decomposers are part of respiration in both bottles.

items.q: Use both bottles to find gross productivity, in mg/L of oxygen per day.

why.correct: Gross = net + respiration $= (9.5 - 8.0) + (8.0 - 7.4) = 1.5 + 0.6 = 2.1$ mg/L per day.

mistakes.why: You subtracted respiration from net. Gross productivity adds it back: 1.5 + 0.6.
1.5 is the net change. Add the respiration from the dark bottle (0.6) to get gross.

items.q: Why is the dark bottle needed in this experiment?
options: It measures respiration by itself.
It shows how much light the algae need to grow.
It keeps the water in the bottles from warming up.
It stops the algae in the bottle from respiring.

why.correct: With no light there is no photosynthesis, so the oxygen drop is respiration. Adding it to the clear-bottle change gives gross productivity.
options: Right: it isolates respiration.
One dark bottle cannot measure light need.
Temperature is not its purpose.
Algae respire in the dark; that is what it measures.
